sum: BYD rolled its 19-millionth new-energy vehicle off the line in Xi'an on Monday, a Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9 that also marked the opening of reservations for the SUV. The production landmark arrived on the same day the company's shares slipped 1.9% to EUR 7.94 — and against a backdrop of European political pressure and a sales mix in which exports are doing the heavy lifting.

A group of 14 members of the European Parliament has asked the European Commission to assess whether BYD vehicles pose potential security risks. According to Reuters, the lawmakers wrote to the Commission on November 4 seeking an examination of the matter and a review of possible restrictions. Among the options they raised was exclusion from public procurement procedures. BYD told Reuters it does not pass European vehicle data to BYD entities or third parties in China.

The political noise sits alongside a solid quarterly report. On October 29, BYD posted third-quarter 2026 revenue of RMB 221 billion, up 13.59% year on year. Net profit attributable to shareholders climbed 28.08% to RMB 10.02 billion, growing faster than the top line. For the first nine months of 2026, revenue reached RMB 566 billion and net profit came in at RMB 22.3 billion.

Sales figures confirmed roughly a week earlier showed about 490,000 vehicles sold worldwide in October, an 11% increase on the same month a year earlier. Overseas deliveries more than doubled, rising 102.8% to around 170,000 units. Reuters reported that growth leaned on foreign markets to offset soft domestic demand and fierce price competition at home. For January through October, BYD sold about 3.62 million vehicles — still 2.16% below the prior-year level despite the October gain.

On the product side, BYD launched the second-generation Seal 07 in China on Thursday, offered as both a battery-electric car and a plug-in hybrid. UOB Kay Hian put the price range at RMB 139,900 to RMB 172,900 in a Thursday note, with the entry price of the battery-electric version 12% below its March level.

BYD's Record October Masks a Profit Gap and a European Roadblock
sum: BYD rolled its 19-millionth new-energy vehicle off the line and opened order books for the Tai 9 SUV under its Fang Cheng Bao sub-brand — with no price attached — but investors greeted the twin milestones coolly. The stock shed 4.0% to €8.20, extending a run of weakness that has left the shares down 3.7% in a single session earlier in the week.

The selling reflects a company pulling in two directions at once. Overseas demand is booming; the home front is contracting; and the bottom line is no longer keeping pace with the top line in the way the market had come to expect.

BYD's third-quarter 2026 report, released on 29 October, showed revenue of RMB 221.488 billion, up 13.59% year on year. Net profit attributable to shareholders climbed 28.08% to RMB 10.020 billion — a faster rate of expansion than sales, which points to improving operating leverage in the quarter.

The market, however, had pencilled in more. Consensus estimates reported by Reuters ranged from RMB 11.4 billion to RMB 12.95 billion, leaving the actual figure short of even the low end. Bloomberg, covering the same release a day later, framed the shortfall against a backdrop of a shrinking domestic auto market and mounting efforts abroad to curb Chinese imports. Competition, by BYD's own account, has intensified both at home and overseas.

Monthly delivery data published on 1 November laid bare the divergence. BYD moved 490,168 new-energy vehicles in October, a gain of 10.97% on the prior-year month. Domestic volume, though, fell 10.6%.

The growth is therefore increasingly an export story. Passenger-car and pick-up sales outside China reached 169,564 units, an increase of 103.0% year on year — roughly double the year-earlier level. Reuters put the overseas figure at about 170,000, up 102.8%, and noted that domestic demand remains soft amid a fierce price war.

Momentum is also cooling at the margin. October's 11% headline increase compares with a 17% jump in September, a deceleration that suggests the home-market drag is beginning to tell on the group total.

BYD's Overseas Sales Jump 91% as R&D Spending Outpaces Profit
sum: BYD is leaning on international markets to offset a shrinking home base, and the numbers for the first nine months of 2026 make the shift plain. Overseas volumes climbed roughly 91% year on year between January and September, while domestic sales fell about 30%. Foreign markets accounted for around 43% of total deliveries in that window, up from roughly 21% a year earlier. All told, the automaker moved about 3.1316 million vehicles over the nine months.

The export surge comes against a backdrop of mounting trade barriers. Import duties on BYD vehicles run from 27% in the EU to 100% in the US, and the company is challenging its US designation in court. Stella Li, BYD's executive vice president, flagged geopolitics as the single biggest hurdle to the group's international build-out and named both the tariffs and the US listing among the obstacles in its path. How well BYD can work around those restrictions will go a long way toward determining whether overseas demand can keep compensating for weakness at home.

The expansion is being funded by a hefty research budget. Executive vice president He Zhiqi said on 1 November that BYD spent 36.3 billion RMB on research and development in the first nine months of 2026 — more than the 22.3 billion RMB net profit it booked over the same period. Cumulative R&D outlays have now passed 280 billion RMB, he added.

Quarterly results, however, landed short of expectations. Net profit for the third quarter of 2026 came in at 10.02 billion yuan, against analyst forecasts of 11.4 billion to 12.95 billion yuan. Revenue of 221.5 billion yuan also disappointed, with higher dealer discounts on older models weighing on average selling prices, according to media reports. Hong Kong-listed shares slipped intraday on 30 October following the release.

October deliveries offered a brighter read. BYD sold about 490,000 new-energy vehicles, up 10.97% from a year earlier, though Reuters noted the pace slowed from September. Exports more than doubled in October, rising 102.8% to roughly 170,000 units, and overseas business helped offset soft domestic demand and fierce price competition. Even so, cumulative sales from January to October stood about 2.16% below the prior-year level, at around 3.6 million vehicles.

The rebound followed a weaker session earlier in the week that media reports tied to Piper Sandler's decision on Tuesday to cut its price target on the Hong Kong-listed automaker from HK$95 to HK$74, while keeping a Neutral rating. The stock recovered alongside other Hong Kong-listed auto names after BYD moved to quash speculation about its in-house intelligent driving systems.

On Wednesday, BYD rejected online claims that production of its "God's Eye C" driver-assistance system had been halted. The company also disputed suggestions that it would swap its self-developed solutions for an outside supplier, affirming its commitment to fully in-house development and pledging to keep updating its own software.

The clarification came as BYD continued to roll out new product. Also on Thursday, according to media reports, the automaker launched the second-generation Seal 07 in China, offered in both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid form. The all-electric version carries a claimed range of 775 kilometers under China's CLTC standard and features BYD's Flash Charging; pricing with trade-in starts at RMB 135,900.

Operationally, BYD reported unaudited figures on November 1 showing roughly 490,000 new-energy vehicles sold in October, a 10.97% increase from a year earlier — down from the 17% growth recorded in September. Exports accounted for about 170,000 units, more than doubling year-on-year with a gain of 102.84%.

Reuters noted that overseas shipments helped offset sluggish domestic demand and fierce price competition in China, where the company has been under pressure. For the January-to-October period, BYD sold approximately 3.6 million vehicles, still 2.16% below the prior-year level despite the October uptick. The denial, carried in media reports, addressed both the future of the systems and the technical responsibility for building them.

BlackRock disclosed an off-exchange sale of BYD H-shares on Tuesday, with media reports putting the reported long position at 6.95%, down from 7.17%. BYD's Autonomous Bus Debut Arrives as Investors Wait on Earnings Proof
sum: BYD rolled out two new buses on a single day, unveiling an autonomous electric model in Singapore and a long-distance coach in Birmingham. The product news lands at an awkward moment for shareholders: the company's sales machine is running hot, but its bottom line has yet to convince the market it can keep pace.

The stock gained 2.3% in the prior session, a move The Business Times tied to strengthening overseas demand for Chinese cars. That enthusiasm has a counterweight. CMB International reaffirmed its buy rating on the Hong Kong-listed shares on 30 October while cutting its price target to HK$109 from HK$125, citing weaker-than-expected quarterly results and sector headwinds. A buy call paired with a lower target is no unconditional endorsement — it is a positive view attached to a reduced valuation yardstick.

The trigger for that reassessment came a day earlier. Reuters reported on 29 October that third-quarter 2026 earnings growth fell short of forecasts. Net profit attributable to shareholders climbed 28% year on year to 10.02 billion yuan, while revenue advanced 13.6% to 221.49 billion yuan. Both figures represent solid expansion. Neither was enough to clear the bar the market had already set.

That gap is the crux of the investment case. A company can grow briskly and still disappoint when expectations were priced higher. Rising revenue and higher profit do not rule out a miss against consensus, and no single quarter's growth figure offers an all-clear on valuation.

October delivery data supply the strongest argument for the optimists. BYD sold 490,168 vehicles worldwide, with exports jumping 102.8% year on year to 170,194 units. The overseas business is expanding fast enough to explain the positive share-price reaction to the sales report.

What it does not yet prove is a matching improvement in profitability. Demand and earnings need to be assessed separately. In the best case, BYD converts that foreign appetite into additional profitable business, turning the sales report into the starting point for a more convincing profit trajectory rather than a one-day trading spark. Delivering more vehicles is not sufficient on its own — the extra volume must contribute enough to close the shortfall against expectations from the past quarter.

sum: BYD reported stronger third-quarter operations on October 29, but the earnings release also showed why investors are watching the company's overseas expansion closely. Net profit rose 28 percent year over year to 10.02 billion yuan, while revenue increased 14 percent to 221.49 billion yuan, according to Morningstar, citing Dow Jones Newswires.

The result remained below expectations. Visible Alpha analysts had projected net profit of 11.10 billion yuan and revenue of 240.83 billion yuan. For the first nine months, net profit fell 4.2 percent to 22.34 billion yuan, while revenue was broadly flat at 566.30 billion yuan. The figures point to a company still growing in absolute terms, but facing a more demanding earnings comparison and heavier competition in China.

Exports were the main counterweight to weaker home-market conditions. BYD shipped more than 550,700 new-energy vehicles in the third quarter, more than double the year-earlier level, and overseas sales represented more than 40 percent of quarterly deliveries. Total vehicle sales rose 19 percent to about 1.3 million units, a much slower pace than the export increase.

The latest monthly data show both the strength and the limits of that strategy. Automotive World reported on November 2 that October deliveries rose 11 percent to 490,168 vehicles, the highest monthly total of 2026 and the sixth consecutive month of growth. Battery-electric passenger-car sales exceeded 300,000 for the first time.

At the same time, October exports reached 170,194 vehicles, up 102.8 percent from a year earlier but lower than in September. Automotive World said exports had declined for a second consecutive month, while domestic sales fell 10.6 percent year over year to 319,974 vehicles. That mix leaves BYD dependent on overseas capacity and continued battery-electric demand as plug-in-hybrid demand weakens.

European trade policy adds another constraint. Chinese plug-in-hybrid imports into the European Union are facing a proposed 2027 limit, increasing the importance of battery-electric models and locally assembled vehicles. BYD is expanding production in Hungary, Thailand, Brazil and Turkey, but those facilities still need to reach scale.

The mix matters too. Of the total, 305,743 were battery-electric passenger cars and 177,382 were plug-in hybrids, so the overall delivery count should not be read as pure EV sales.

Analysts had expected more: estimates ranged from RMB11.4 billion to RMB12.95 billion. Revenue for the quarter came in at RMB221.49 billion, a gain of 13.59%.

Those two data points are not in conflict. They simply use different yardsticks — growth against the prior year versus the bar set by the market. A 28% increase and a missed consensus can both be true at once.
The longer view is less flattering. Across the first nine months of 2026, net profit fell 4.24% to RMB22.34 billion, meaning the third-quarter rebound has not yet offset the weaker start to the year.

Beneath the 10.97% year-on-year gain — and a 5.74% sequential rise that marked the sixth consecutive month of annual growth — the Chinese automaker's lineup is pulling in two directions at once.

Battery-electric passenger cars hit 305,743 units, up 37.38% from a year earlier and the third straight monthly record. Plug-in hybrids, by contrast, slid 17.23%. The divergence means the group's overall momentum rests almost entirely on its pure-electric range, with hybrid weakness offset at the consolidated level rather than cured.

Geography reinforces the imbalance. Domestic sales came in at 319,974 vehicles, down 10.57% year on year, as soft demand and fierce price competition weighed on the home market, according to Reuters. Exports told the opposite story: 170,194 units shipped abroad, a jump of 102.84%. That overseas surge has become the main counterweight to China's slowdown — though Reuters also flags the possibility of fresh EU restrictions on BYD hybrid imports under a China-EU trade arrangement, a risk rather than a confirmed hit.

For the year to date, the picture is still one of repair rather than recovery. Cumulative January-to-October volume reached 3,621,744 new-energy vehicles, 2.16% below the same period a year earlier. October's strength has not yet erased that deficit.

The sales release landed a day after BYD's third-quarter report, which showed net profit up 28.08% year on year to RMB 10.02 billion. Solid growth on paper — but not enough to clear expectations. Broker estimates compiled by Reuters had ranged from RMB 11.4 billion to RMB 12.95 billion, leaving even the low end out of reach. Reuters also pointed to margin pressure from the intense domestic competitive battle.

sum: BYD shares climbed 4.6% on Thursday, with the advance coming despite — not because of — a fresh access restriction at a US military installation. The gain tracked a broader recovery in Hong Kong tech and EV names, mirroring a 4.4% rise the prior session as selling pressure on the sector eased. Battery and electric-vehicle peers including CATL joined the move, a pattern that points to market-wide sentiment rather than any single company catalyst.

That distinction matters. A friendlier tape can support a share price without answering the harder question of how demand and operations are actually developing. For that, investors have to look at delivery data, expansion plans and the barriers now appearing in BYD's path.

From October 26, vehicles made by BYD will be barred from Kadena Air Base on Okinawa. According to Reuters, the prohibition covers private cars as well as taxis, delivery vans, and contracted and commercial vehicles. Base spokesperson Lt.-Col. Alli Stormer called the vehicles an "unacceptable and unavoidable risk" to personnel and mission. The base did not specify what triggered the decision, and BYD did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The scope of the restriction is the variable that counts. A single installation's rule is a far cry from limits imposed on larger customer groups. Yonhap has reported concerns that cameras and sensors could capture and transmit sensitive military information, and media reports float the possibility of extending similar rules to other US bases in Japan and South Korea. US Forces Korea, however, said it currently has no changes to its access rules to announce.

The political backdrop stretches beyond Okinawa. The Pentagon listed BYD in June among companies it says support China's military — a designation BYD rejects. Security allegations and proven misconduct are separate matters, though the practical restrictions that could flow from such listings are what matter for valuation.

Against that friction, BYD's sales machine keeps running. Reuters reported on October 1 that worldwide vehicle sales rose for a fifth straight month, with exports offsetting persistently weak demand at home. The two trends sit side by side: global volume growing while the domestic business struggles.

sum: BYD shares climbed 3.8% on Thursday, riding a broader recovery in Chinese battery and automaker stocks that also lifted peer CATL. The advance came as investors weighed a pair of product stories against a more cautious earnings backdrop from Wall Street.

The move was sector-wide rather than company-specific. Expectations of a year-end export push and an improving sales trend across the industry underpinned sentiment, though neither constitutes a reported order intake for BYD itself. A rising tide for the sector does not translate directly into the fortunes of any single manufacturer, and the stock's gain should be read alongside the parallel recovery in other lithium-battery names in Hong Kong.

On the product front, BYD has launched the new Seagull in five trim levels, priced from RMB 65,900 to RMB 99,900. The headline feature is fast-charging capability built around the second-generation Blade Battery. The company has not drawn a causal link between the model's debut and the share-price move, and none is established.

Sitting above the Seagull in the lineup is the Great Han, an electric flagship sedan unveiled in China. Media reports credit it with a range exceeding 1,000 kilometers, along with fast-charging capability. An earlier report on October 16 had put the Great Han's range at more than 500 miles. Both figures are range claims rather than verified real-world results.

Regulatory filings added further detail to the pipeline. An October 17 publication from China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology disclosed dimensions and powertrain specifications for the all-new Han and the third-generation Qin Plus. Such disclosures flesh out the model program but do not amount to a market launch, and the technical specifications matter less than how quickly the vehicles reach showrooms.

The two models strike different notes: the Seagull emphasizes entry-level pricing and new charging technology, while the Great Han serves as a flagship halo product. Neither offers a clear read-through to earnings, and a new offering is not proof of incremental sales or higher margins.
That distinction matters given the analyst view. Goldman Sachs reaffirmed its buy rating on BYD on October 15 and kept its price target at HK$134 — neither a fresh upgrade nor a raised target.

sum: Lucid Group LCID, a California-based maker of high-end battery electric vehicles, faced extreme stock volatility this week after an obscure EV blog claimed the company was considering bankruptcy. The report triggered a 57% intraday plunge on Tuesday, although Lucid denied that it was planning a Chapter 11 filing after hiring a strategic adviser. The shares recovered the entire decline and more by Wednesday, but the episode highlighted investor concerns surrounding the company's cash burn, management changes and job reductions. Lucid delivered fewer than 4,000 vehicles during the second quarter and appears to have sufficient liquidity through this year, while free cash flow is not expected to become positive before 2030. This outlook suggests Lucid may need additional external financing, leaving its future closely connected to Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, which owns more than half of its equity and has also provided loans.

Lucid's factory in Saudi Arabia could provide an incentive for continued support, although the company's market value has fallen from more than $91 billion in 2021 to approximately $2.3 billion. Rivian Automotive, another electric-vehicle startup, appears to be in a stronger position but has also secured outside funding from Volkswagen, a foreign company that has become its largest shareholder, as Rivian works toward greater scale. Rivian's valuation has declined from more than $150 billion to around $26 billion, reflecting the broader reset experienced by electric-vehicle startups after earlier enthusiasm drove valuations higher. Lordstown Motors and Fisker, two other electric-vehicle companies, have already entered bankruptcy, and their failures show how expensive and challenging it may be for new automakers to build sufficient production scale. Investors may therefore view Lucid's difficulties as part of a wider problem for the U.S. electric-vehicle startup ecosystem rather than an isolated setback for one small manufacturer.

BYD's August Sales Record Conceals a Widening Domestic-International Divide
sum: The Chinese electric vehicle giant keeps shipping more cars than ever, yet its share price tells a far more cautious story. BYD delivered 440,293 new-energy vehicles in August, marking a fourth consecutive month of growth and a 17.8 percent year-on-year improvement. The stock, however, closed the week at €9.45 in one session and has since drifted to €9.29 — a decline of roughly 8 percent over the past month that leaves the equity trading about a quarter below its 52-week peak.

What makes the August numbers remarkable is where the growth originated. Overseas deliveries surged 134.5 percent to 189,466 vehicles, and the cumulative international tally for the first eight months reached 1,162,260 units — an 86 percent jump that now accounts for nearly 44 percent of BYD's total annual volume. Company figures show that international markets generated more than half of revenue in the first half of the year, a first for the automaker.

The pure-electric segment hit its own milestone: 256,230 battery-electric vehicles sold in August, the first time BYD has crossed the 250,000 mark in a single month, representing 28.4 percent growth year on year. Commercial new-energy vehicles also showed momentum, with sales climbing 225 percent to 6,909 units while electric bus deliveries rose 51.8 percent.

The domestic picture remains the counterweight to all this overseas optimism. August sales in China fell 14.34 percent to 250,827 vehicles, and the eight-month cumulative decline stands at 6.84 percent across 2,668,015 units. Encouragingly, the pace of contraction has moderated considerably from the first half, when domestic sales were down 15.72 percent.

That split personality extends to the financial statements. Second-quarter net profit rose 29.8 percent to 8.2 billion yuan, snapping a four-quarter streak of earnings declines. But revenue slipped 3.2 percent to 194.6 billion yuan — a fourth consecutive quarterly drop — and the profit figure fell well short of the roughly 48 percent consensus increase analysts had penciled in. The board formally approved the half-year results, which cover the period through June 30, in late August.
The rapid global push by Chinese automakers, with BYD at the forefront, has not gone unnoticed by regulators.

sum: Electric vehicle brand Tesla topped the import car market in the first half of the year with a market share of more than 30%. With another EV brand BYD also seeing its first-half sales surge more than 800% from a year earlier, EVs accounted for nearly half of the overall imported car market.

According to the Korea Automobile Importers & Distributors Association (KAIDA) on July 3, cumulative new registrations of imported passenger cars from January to June this year came to 184,032, up 33.2% from the same period last year (138,120). Sales in June alone were 38,059, up 37% from a year earlier.

By brand, Tesla sold 55,139 units in the first half, taking 30.5% of the total market. Sales jumped 192.2% from a year earlier, and its share widened by 16.6 percentage points. It ranked No. 1 among all brands.

BMW ranked second with a 21.3% market share. It sold 39,150 units in the first half, up 2.3% from the same period last year. No. 3 Mercedes-Benz (16.2% share) sold 29,776 units, down 8.6%. BMW and Mercedes' shares shrank by 6.5 percentage points and 7.4 percentage points, respectively, from a year earlier.
BYD, which entered Korea last year, sold 11,675 units. That figure skyrocketed 807.9% from a year earlier. Its market share also expanded sharply from 0.93% to 6.34%, ranking fourth.
Other top sellers were Lexus (7,819 units), Volvo (7,470), Audi (7,337), Toyota (5,187), Porsche (4,322) and Mini (4,091).

Here's the good news for investors: BYD is aware of its issues and has a plan to turn things around. Part of the company's goal is to export the strategy that made it so successful in China to other places. BYD became one of the top EV companies in China -- the largest market in the world -- thanks to its vertically integrated approach, differentiated battery technology (it was originally a battery maker), and focus on offering affordable, mass market vehicles that saw significant adoption.

BYD has been aggressively expanding into other countries. The company plans to sell 50% of its cars outside of China by 2030. The U.S. may not be one of those countries BYD targets, as the company's imports would be subject to significant tariffs. sum: The stability of electric vehicle fires is once again under fire due to an unexpected fire accident in the parking lot of BYD headquarters. In addition, large-scale topics caused BYD Hong Kong shares to fall at one point, shaking financial markets.

On the afternoon of the 14th, the fire, which started at a parking facility affiliated with BYD headquarters in China, quickly spread with black smoke and was fortunately contained by firefighters dispatched to the scene. Fortunately, no casualties have been confirmed so far, but the physical damage has been considerable, with dozens of parked vehicles being burned down, and the accident seems to cause more than just a fire.

Above all, the place where the fire broke out is attracting attention from the industry in that it is the parking lot of the headquarters, which is the heart of BYD. In particular, BYD has emphasized the overwhelming fire safety of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries with "blade batteries." The accident is expected to deal a significant blow to brand credibility. In the market, sharp debates are going on over whether the cause of the fire is a defect in the battery system of the vehicle itself or external facilities. If it turns out to be a technical defect, it is expected that a full revision of the safety promotion strategy will be inevitable along with pressure for recalls in the global market.

Financial markets also reacted immediately. As soon as the fire was reported, BYD's stock price in major markets, including the Hong Kong stock market, remained weak throughout the day, reflecting investor anxiety. Investors are concerned that the incident may further dampen consumer sentiment in the "Casms" section, a period of stagnant global electric vehicle demand, and are also closely watching the possibility of a brake on accelerating entry into areas where safety regulations are strict, such as North America and Europe.

BYD said in an immediate statement that it is working with fire authorities to determine the exact cause of the fire. The company is in a position to conduct an objective investigation with all possibilities open and disclose the results transparently.

sum: The arithmetic facing BYD in the second half of the year is unforgiving. To land within its 5 to 5.5 million vehicle sales target for 2026, the Chinese electric vehicle giant must move roughly 530,000 units per month on average — a pace that even July's record-breaking performance fell short of. That tension between overseas momentum and domestic stagnation is now the defining storyline for the company, both on the factory floor and at the trading desk.

July delivered 419,211 vehicle sales, a 21.8 percent jump year over year and a 62nd consecutive month atop China's new energy vehicle sales chart. The headline number, however, flatters the underlying picture. Exports of passenger cars and pickups surged 124.3 percent to 179,841 units, pushing overseas shipments past 40 percent of total volume for the first time. In the first seven months of the year, international sales have accumulated to roughly 969,000 vehicles out of a total of about 2.22 million.

Domestic demand tells a different story. Home-market sales rose just 3 percent month over month, and the broader Chinese auto market contracted 4.1 percent in the first half to around 15 million vehicles. The industry-wide pattern is stark: domestic sales fell 21.1 percent while exports climbed 65.3 percent nationally. BYD's average selling price has dropped 8 percent since the start of the year, a direct consequence of the price war raging on its home turf. Rivals are feeling the same squeeze — Xpeng, Nio and Li Auto all posted month-over-month declines in July, while Geely and Chery leaned even harder into export markets.

The overseas push is gaining traction in markets that were once considered difficult terrain. In South Korea, BYD delivered 11,675 vehicles in the first half of 2026 — nearly double the 6,107 units sold in all of 2025 — in a market long dominated by entrenched domestic manufacturers. The company's appeal to younger, price-conscious buyers appears to be translating well beyond China's borders.

Europe offers an even more striking benchmark. Across the EU, EFTA nations and the UK, BYD's market share more than doubled to 2.4 percent in the first half, pulling level with Tesla for the first time.

sum: According to data from the China Passenger Car Association, CATL achieved a market share of 50.1% in the electric vehicle battery sector in the first quarter of 2026. This figure represents CATL’s estimated production share in the domestic market. It is an estimate, as the first quarter has not yet concluded—five days remain in March.

Regardless, the portal Car News China reports that CATL has regained this level of dominance in China for the first time in five years. In 2021, the company already held half of the domestic market, which at the time had a significantly smaller total volume. Incidentally, China’s total production volume of EV batteries for the first two months of the year reached 310 GWh, representing a 22% increase compared to the previous year.
But Car News China emphasises: “However, the proportion between produced and installed packs reached the historical low of 19%.” Currently, a significant volume is being produced for stock.

What stands out is CATL’s strategic positioning: the company dominates the ternary NMC battery segment in China while simultaneously expanding its presence in the LFP segment. The figures reflect this: CATL’s market share for NMC batteries reached 81.6% between January and March. Its market share for LFP batteries stood at 41% in the first quarter—’the highest [level] in four years,’ according to Car News China.

As the table shows, CATL leads by a significant margin. The second-largest domestic battery manufacturer in the first quarter was BYD, with a 17.5% market share, representing a 4.3% decline compared to the previous year. Car News China describes this as BYD’s ‘weakest result in five years.’ However, the company, which operates solely in the LFP segment, holds a 22.6% share of the LFP battery market. In this segment, the gap to CATL is not as pronounced.

Overall, it is clear that most manufacturers focus on either NMC or LFP battery chemistries. Only CATL and CALB pursue a dual strategy, while other manufacturers largely concentrate on a single chemistry—more frequently LFP than NMC. Consequently, the LFP market is more competitive, whereas CATL has pulled far ahead in the NMC battery segment with the aforementioned 81% market share. Only SVOLT and CALB still hold market shares above 5%.

items.t: 2025 Was a Turning Point for BYD. Here's What Investors Must Know.
sum: For years, BYD's (BYDDY -1.20%) investment story was easy to summarize: a Chinese EV champion benefiting from scale, cost advantages, and early bets on electrification.

But 2025 marked a clear shift. BYD didn't just grow bigger; it grew more complex. The company crossed a critical threshold, transitioning from a domestic leader to a global player, while also revealing the next set of challenges investors must address.
If you strip away the headlines and focus on what actually matters, three developments define BYD's 2025 story.

The most crucial change in 2025 is that BYD stopped being "China-first" in practice, not just ambition. Export volumes surged, overseas sales accelerated, and Europe emerged as a meaningful growth market rather than a test case. BYD is now on track to export close to 1 million vehicles annually, a scale that few automakers achieve outside their home markets.

This matters because China's EV market is maturing fast. Competition is intense, pricing pressure is relentless, and growth is no longer guaranteed. By expanding aggressively abroad, BYD is diversifying its revenue base and reducing its dependence on a single market.

More importantly, the expansion isn't limited to shipping cars overseas. BYD is localizing its production, building factories in regions such as Southeast Asia, Europe, and Latin America. That positions the company to sidestep tariffs, shorten supply chains, and embed itself more deeply in local markets.
For investors, this global push expands BYD's long-term opportunity set. The company is no longer constrained by China's demand curve alone -- it's now competing for a share of global EV adoption.

Is BYD Stock a Millionaire Maker?
sum: BYD (BYDDY -1.20%), China's largest automaker, has minted a lot of millionaires since its public debut in 2002. A $10,000 investment in its Hong Kong IPO would be worth $1.07 million today.

That rally was driven by its evolution from a battery maker into an automaker, and its expansion into the electric vehicle (EV) market. Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, which invested in BYD in 2008, also reaped some big profits from the automaker before closing out its position earlier this year.

But with a market cap of $122 billion, BYD is still less valuable than Tesla ($1.43 trillion), Toyota ($270 billion), and other multinational automakers. Could it soar even higher and churn a fresh $10,000 investment into $1 million over the long term?

BYD was originally a battery manufacturer. It expanded into the automaking market in 2003, and it launched its first gas-powered vehicles in 2005. It introduced its first battery-powered EDV, the BYD e6, in 2009 -- but it still mainly sold gas-powered vehicles over the following decade.

BYD's auto sales stalled from 2009 to 2020. Its annual shipments still hovered around half a million vehicles, but it struggled to gain new customers as it grappled with tougher competition, quality control issues, and the market shift toward EVs and other new energy vehicles (NEVs).

To break out of that rut, BYD expanded its NEV business with new battery-powered electric vehicles (BEVs) powered by its own lithium iron phosphate (LFP) "Blade" batteries. These batteries gave it an edge against other EV makers because they were generally safer, cheaper, and more power-efficient than traditional lithium-ion batteries.

BYD also revamped its vehicle designs, increased its production capacity, slashed its prices, and expanded beyond China into Southeast Asia, Latin America, and Europe. It vertically integrated its own supply chain to reduce its production costs, unified its fragmented production lines under its e-Platform 3.0 architecture, and sold a higher mix of higher-margin plug-in hybrid vehicles (PHEVs) to stabilize its gross margins. It also became the first major automaker to completely stop selling gas-powered vehicles in 2022.
